title: God Remembers Noah and Renews the Earth
summary: God remembers Noah, the waters withdraw, the family leaves the ark at His word, and Noah’s offering draws God’s pledge to preserve the earth’s seasons.
historicalContext: Genesis 8 continues the record of a single year in the life of Noah, dated by the patriarch’s own age from the six hundredth year, second month, seventeenth day (7:11) to the six hundred and first year, second month, twenty-seventh day (8:14). The dates read like a ship’s log and assume months of thirty days, since five months equal the one hundred and fifty days of 7:24. The ark grounds in the highlands of Ararat, the region later known as Urartu, north of Assyria in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia. Mesopotamian flood stories also sent out birds and described a sacrifice afterward, but Genesis stands apart from them: one God rules the waters, no deity is hungry for food, the hero carries no crew, and the account closes with a promise of steady seasons for the whole inhabited earth rather than with gods quarrelling over a mistake.
literaryContext: The flood narrative of Genesis 6:9–9:29 turns on the words “God remembered Noah” (8:1). Before that sentence the waters rise, the mountains disappear, and every breathing creature outside the ark dies; after it the movements reverse in nearly the same order. The waters stop, recede, and uncover the hills; birds go out; the family and animals leave; worship follows. The chapter deliberately retells Genesis 1: a wind passes over the waters, the waters are bounded, dry ground appears, plants grow, birds and land creatures receive the command to multiply, and human beings stand again on a cleansed earth. Noah, who has not spoken once in the story, acts by obedience and worship. The chapter closes in God’s own heart (8:21–22), preparing for the spoken covenant and the rainbow of chapter 9, and it echoes the earlier verdict on the human heart (6:5) to show that grace, not changed human nature, carries the world forward.
themes: God’s covenant remembrance as the turning point of judgment
Re-creation after the undoing of the world
Worship as the first act on a renewed earth
Sacrifice, acceptance, and grace toward sinful humanity
God’s faithfulness in the order of the seasons

outline.title: God Remembers and the Waters Withdraw
outline.summary: God sends a wind, seals the sources of the flood, and the ark settles on the mountains of Ararat as the peaks reappear.

outline.title: The Raven, the Dove, and the Olive Leaf
outline.summary: Noah opens the window and tests the earth by sending birds until the dove brings a fresh olive leaf and finally does not return.

outline.title: Dry Ground and the Command to Go Forth
outline.summary: Noah sees the dry ground but waits for God’s command, then leads his family and every creature out of the ark to multiply on the earth.

outline.title: The Altar and God’s Pledge
outline.summary: Noah offers clean animals as burnt offerings, and the LORD accepts them and resolves never again to strike all life, guaranteeing the seasons while the earth remains.

verses.bibleText: And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The flood narrative pivots on four Hebrew words: “And God remembered Noah.” Up to this point the waters have risen, the hills have vanished, and every breathing creature outside the ark has perished (7:21–23). From here the movement runs the other way. The sentence does not suggest that God had lost track of the ark for five months and suddenly recalled it. In Scripture, when God remembers, He acts on a commitment already made. He remembered His covenant and heard Israel’s groaning in Egypt (Exodus 2:24); He remembered Abraham and brought Lot out of Sodom (Genesis 19:29); He remembered Rachel and opened her womb (30:22). Here the commitment is the covenant promised in 6:18, and the action is deliverance from death.

The verse is careful about what God remembered. It does not say He recalled Noah’s righteousness, as though the turn of the story were a reward. It names Noah, then “every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark.” The animals share in the remembrance. The God who, Jesus said, does not forget a single sparrow (Luke 12:6–7) kept the whole floating household in mind, beasts as well as people. Such care for creatures gives weight to the later assurance that His children are worth more than many sparrows.

Remembrance becomes action at once: “God made a wind to pass over the earth.” The Hebrew word for wind is the same word used for the Spirit of God moving over the waters in 1:2. The echo is intended. The world has been returned to something like its condition before the first day, with water covering everything, and now God begins again as He began then, sending His wind across the deep. What follows in the chapter mirrors creation: waters separated and bounded, dry land appearing, plants springing up, birds and animals released to multiply, and human beings set on the ground to worship.

“The waters asswaged.” The verb pictures something settling down after agitation, the way anger cools. The flood was never a blind force of nature. It came at God’s word and it subsides at His word. For anyone who has waited through a long season that felt like abandonment, the verse holds out the same truth Noah lived: the God who seems silent has not stopped keeping His promise, and His remembering always moves toward rescue.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים (wayyizkor ʾelohim) — and God remembered
wordNotes.explanation: The verb zakar with God as subject describes purposeful action toward someone on the basis of a prior commitment, not the recovery of a lapsed memory. The same verb opens the Sabbath commandment (“Remember the sabbath day”), where it also calls for active observance. In Genesis it marks moments when God intervenes to save from death or barrenness.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּשֹׁכּוּ (wayyashokku) — and (the waters) asswaged
wordNotes.explanation: The verb shakak means to subside or grow calm. Outside this verse it describes the cooling of a king’s wrath (Esther 2:1; 7:10). Its use here quietly links the falling waters with the easing of judgment, though the narrative keeps the focus on the physical withdrawal of the flood.

verses.bibleText: The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The flood had two sources, named when it began: “all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened” (7:11). Now both are shut. The subterranean waters and the waters from above are “stopped,” and the rain is “restrained.” The verbs are passive, as the opening verbs of 7:11 were passive. That pairing makes a point the narrator wants no reader to miss: the opening and the closing of the floodgates were both the work of God. Nothing in the account credits the sun, a storm deity, or the exhaustion of the clouds.

The verse may describe what had already happened before the waters began to recede in verse 1. Read that way, verse 1 gives the effect and verse 2 the underlying cause: once the sources were sealed, the wind could do its work. Either way, the passage shows God governing both the duration and the end of the judgment.

The imagery of bounded waters recalls the second and third days of creation, when God divided the waters and gathered them into their place (1:6–10). Job and the Psalms later celebrate the same authority, describing the Lord who shut up the sea with doors and set it a limit it cannot pass (Job 38:8–11; Psalm 104:9). The God who restrained the flood still restrains the forces that threaten His people.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּסָּכְרוּ … וַיִּכָּלֵא (wayyissakru … wayyikkale) — were stopped … was restrained
wordNotes.explanation: Both verbs are passive, matching the passive “were broken up” and “were opened” of 7:11. The first means to be closed or dammed up; the second, to be held back or confined, as when rain is withheld or a person is shut in. Together they present the end of the flood as divinely controlled from start to finish.

verses.bibleText: And the waters returned from off the earth continually: and after the end of the hundred and fifty days the waters were abated.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The recession was gradual. The KJV’s “returned … continually” renders a Hebrew idiom of going and returning, a steady back-and-forth retreat like a tide that withdraws a little further each time. The waters were not annihilated; they went back to the places God had assigned them, above and below the earth.

“After the end of the hundred and fifty days the waters were abated.” This number matches the one hundred and fifty days the waters “prevailed” in 7:24, measured from the start of the flood. The two references together bracket the climax of the narrative. The phrase best describes the beginning of a noticeable decrease at that point, since verse 5 shows the waters still diminishing for months afterward.

The careful counting reflects an account that treats these events as real history. Five months of thirty days each bring the reader to the very date in the next verse when the ark touches ground. The precision speaks of a God who measures judgment and deliverance alike, and whose timetable does not drift.

wordNotes.term: הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב (halokh washov) — continually (literally “going and returning”)
wordNotes.explanation: Two infinitives joined together express ongoing, repeated action. Here they picture waters moving back and forth as they recede, a slow and progressive withdrawal rather than a sudden drop. A similar construction in verse 5 (“going and decreasing”) continues the description.

verses.bibleText: And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month.” The flood began on the seventeenth day of the second month (7:11); exactly five months later the ark comes to rest. With thirty-day months, this equals the one hundred and fifty days of verse 3 and 7:24. The narrator gives the date with care but the place only broadly: “upon the mountains of Ararat.” Scripture names a region, not a particular summit.

Ararat is the land later called Urartu, a mountainous kingdom north of Assyria, roughly the area of modern Armenia and eastern Turkey. Elsewhere in the Old Testament it appears as a place of refuge for the assassins of Sennacherib (2 Kings 19:37) and as a kingdom summoned against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27). The high peak now called Mount Ararat rises nearly seventeen thousand feet, and the range as a whole offered a fitting landing place from which the survivors could later spread in every direction. Claims to have found the remains of the ark have not been confirmed, and the text shows no interest in marking the spot for pilgrimage.

The verb “rested” carries a play on Noah’s name. Lamech had named his son Noah, saying, “This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands, because of the ground which the LORD hath cursed” (5:29). The name sounds like the Hebrew word for rest. Now the ark, carrying Noah, “rests.” The same root reappears when the dove finds no “rest” (8:9) and when the LORD smells a “sweet savour,” literally an aroma of rest (8:21). Through Noah God begins to bring a measure of rest to a world under the curse.

That rest was provisional. The full rest Lamech longed for would come only through the One who said, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The ark grounded on a mountain still surrounded by water; the believer’s rest in Christ is real now, yet still awaits the day when the earth itself is made new.

wordNotes.term: וַתָּנַח (wattanach) — and (the ark) rested
wordNotes.explanation: From nuach, “to settle, come to rest,” the verb sounds like the name Noah (noach). The same root names God’s resting on the seventh day in Exodus 20:11. In this context it describes the ark settling onto solid ground, while the wordplay ties the event to the hope of rest attached to Noah’s birth.

wordNotes.term: הָרֵי אֲרָרָט (hare ʾararat) — the mountains of Ararat
wordNotes.explanation: The plural “mountains” refers to a range or region, so the phrase may mean “one of the mountains of Ararat.” Ararat corresponds to the ancient kingdom of Urartu in the highlands north of Mesopotamia. The text fixes the date precisely but leaves the exact peak unnamed.

verses.bibleText: And the waters decreased continually until the tenth month: in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, were the tops of the mountains seen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The waters kept going down for two and a half more months. On the first day of the tenth month “were the tops of the mountains seen.” The phrase answers 7:19–20, where “all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.” What had been submerged is now uncovered, step by step, as the dry land of the third day of creation emerged from the deep (1:9).

The ark had already grounded two months earlier, which suggests it settled on a high ridge while neighbouring peaks still lay beneath the surface. From the ark’s small openings Noah could see only so far; the gradual appearance of other summits around him marked the steady fall of the waters. The language of mountaintops reappearing across the horizon fits a flood that had covered the earth, not a local overflow in a river valley.

Noah had now spent more than seven months afloat and aground. The slowness itself is instructive. God could have dried the earth in a moment, yet He chose a process that required the family to keep trusting through long weeks with little to see but water and distant peaks.

wordNotes.term: רָאשֵׁי הֶהָרִים (rashe heharim) — the tops of the mountains
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the heads of the mountains,” the same summits that 7:20 says the waters covered by fifteen cubits. Their reappearance reverses the climax of the flood and marks the beginning of a habitable earth.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass at the end of forty days, that Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Forty days after the mountaintops appeared, Noah “opened the window of the ark which he had made.” The number forty, which measured the falling rain (7:12, 17), now measures a season of waiting on the far side of the flood. Noah does not throw open the door in the side of the ark (6:16). He opens a smaller opening, apparently high in the structure, to gather information without exposing the household.

The detail shows a man acting with prudence inside God’s providence. God had told him when to enter the ark but had not yet told him when to leave. In the meantime Noah uses the means within reach to learn what he can, while leaving the decision about departure with the One who shut the door (7:16). Faith and careful observation are not rivals here; Noah watches and waits together.

wordNotes.term: חַלּוֹן (challon) — window
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary Hebrew word for a window or opening in a wall, used of Rahab’s window and Daniel’s open windows toward Jerusalem. It differs from the term tsohar in 6:16, which describes the lighting space of the ark. Here it is an opening Noah can unfasten to release the birds.

verses.bibleText: And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first bird released is a raven. It “went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.” The Hebrew repeats the idiom of going out and returning, picturing a bird that ranges back and forth over the water without settling back into the ark for good. A raven is strong, hardy, and able to feed on carrion; it could survive outside the ark on floating remains and exposed peaks long before the lowlands were habitable. Its behaviour therefore told Noah little except that the world was not yet ready.

The choice of a raven first and a dove afterward makes practical sense. The tougher bird could tolerate harsh conditions; the gentler, low-flying dove would reveal whether valleys and trees had emerged. The Mesopotamian flood story reverses the order, sending a dove before a raven, which makes less sense of the birds’ habits. Genesis reads like the record of someone who knew how these creatures behave.

The raven was later listed among unclean birds (Leviticus 11:15; Deuteronomy 14:14), while the dove was clean and could be offered in sacrifice. The narrative itself has already distinguished clean and unclean animals before the flood (7:2), so the contrast between these two birds would not be lost on later readers. The raven goes its own way and never brings back a message; the dove returns, waits, and finally carries a sign of life. Yet God also cares for ravens (Psalm 147:9; Luke 12:24), and the text does not cast this bird as evil. It simply was not the messenger Noah needed.

The phrase “until the waters were dried up” looks ahead to the end of the process. It summarizes the raven’s whole wandering period in one stroke, so the narrator can then return to tell the more detailed story of the dove.

wordNotes.term: עֹרֵב (ʿorev) — raven
wordNotes.explanation: A large black bird of the crow family, a scavenger able to live on carrion. Leviticus places it among birds not to be eaten. Scripture still presents God as feeding ravens and using them to feed Elijah, so the bird’s uncleanness concerns diet and ritual, not divine contempt.

wordNotes.term: יָצוֹא וָשׁוֹב (yatso washov) — to and fro
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “going out and returning,” an idiom of repeated movement. The raven kept flying out and coming back, perhaps resting on the ark’s roof, without ever being taken back inside or bringing news. The same back-and-forth construction described the receding waters in verse 3.

verses.bibleText: Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Noah next “sent forth a dove from him.” The phrase “from him” places the bird close to Noah’s hand, released by the man himself rather than merely let loose. The purpose is stated plainly: “to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground.” Where the raven’s flight had no defined task, the dove is given a mission, and the rest of the story turns on whether that mission is fulfilled.

The dove was suited to it. It feeds on seeds and vegetation, roosts in trees and clefts of rock, and does not live on carrion. If it could find a resting place and food, the lower ground was beginning to recover. Its gentleness made it an apt picture in later Scripture of innocence and devotion (Song of Solomon 2:14; Matthew 10:16), and it was one of the birds permitted for sacrifice (Leviticus 1:14).

The verse uses a verb for “abated” that means to become light or slight. The waters had been heavy upon the earth; Noah wants to know if their weight has lifted. The same Hebrew root returns in verse 21, where the LORD promises not again to “curse” the ground, a word built on the idea of treating something as light or contemptible. The verbal echo hints that the lightening of the waters and the lifting of the threat of judgment belong together.

wordNotes.term: יוֹנָה (yonah) — dove
wordNotes.explanation: The common word for dove or pigeon, also the name of the prophet Jonah. Doves were clean birds, acceptable in sacrifice for those who could not afford larger animals. Their gentleness and habit of returning to their roost made them fitting messengers for Noah.

wordNotes.term: הֲקַלּוּ (haqallu) — (whether the waters) were abated
wordNotes.explanation: From qalal, “to be light, slight, diminished.” The waters were growing lighter on the earth. In its intensive form the same root means to treat as light or to curse, which is the verb in 8:21, linking the easing of the flood with God’s resolve to withhold further destruction.

verses.bibleText: But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth: then he put forth his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The dove “found no rest for the sole of her foot.” Water still covered the lowlands, “on the face of the whole earth,” and the bird returned to the only refuge available. The phrase “the whole earth” keeps the scope of the flood before the reader even as it recedes: there was nowhere for a valley bird to land.

The word translated “rest” again plays on Noah’s name. The ark had found rest on the mountains (8:4), but the dove found none outside. The same wording later describes Israel scattered among the nations: “among these nations shalt thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest” (Deuteronomy 28:65). Outside God’s appointed shelter, there is no settled place. Naomi used a related word when she prayed that her daughters-in-law would find rest in a husband’s house (Ruth 1:9), and the psalmist longed for wings like a dove to fly away and be at rest (Psalm 55:6).

The narrative slows sharply to describe what Noah does next: “he put forth his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark.” Three verbs trace a single tender gesture. After weeks compressed into a sentence, the reader watches one man reach out to one small bird. Noah’s care for this creature reflects the God who had remembered “every living thing” in the ark (8:1) and who later taught that a righteous man regards the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10).

The image of a weary creature drawn back into the place of safety has spoken to believers through the centuries. Christ described Himself as longing to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood (Matthew 23:37). The ark was God’s provided refuge, and the hand that brought the dove in is a small picture of the welcome God extends to those who have found no rest elsewhere.

wordNotes.term: מָנוֹחַ (manoach) — rest (resting place)
wordNotes.explanation: A noun from nuach, “to rest,” meaning a place of settled repose. It echoes the name Noah and the ark’s resting in 8:4. In Ruth 3:1 Naomi seeks “rest” for Ruth, a secure home; in Lamentations Judah among the nations finds none. The dove’s lack of a resting place shows the earth was not yet habitable.

wordNotes.term: כַּף־רַגְלָהּ (kaf-raglah) — the sole of her foot
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the palm of her foot,” a phrase used for setting foot on land. God promised Israel every place the sole of their foot would tread. Here the dove cannot set down even its small foot, a vivid measure of how much water remained.

verses.bibleText: And he stayed yet other seven days; and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he stayed yet other seven days.” The word “other” implies that Noah had already waited seven days before the first release of the dove, so the birds go out on a weekly rhythm. The seven-day pattern appears earlier in the flood story as well, when God gave seven days’ notice before the rain (7:4, 10). The week that God established at creation (2:1–3) still structures time for Noah, long before Israel stood at Sinai.

The verb for waiting suggests patient expectation, the kind of waiting that hopes for an outcome without forcing it. Noah does not grow restless and send the dove every day. He keeps the measured interval and tries again.

wordNotes.term: וַיָּחֶל (wayyachel) — and he stayed (waited)
wordNotes.explanation: From a verb meaning to wait or tarry, closely related to the word for hopeful waiting used of those who wait for the LORD. Noah’s pause is not idle delay; it is the patient expectancy of someone who believes the outcome is in God’s hands.

verses.bibleText: And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
On the second flight the dove stayed out the whole day and “came in to him in the evening.” The longer absence already suggested that she had found somewhere to perch. Then came the surprise the narrator signals with “lo”: “in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off.” The Hebrew describes a leaf freshly torn from a living branch, not a piece of debris floating on the surface. An olive tree somewhere below the mountains had survived and was putting out new growth.

Olive trees grow at moderate elevations, not on high peaks. A green olive leaf meant that the waters had fallen far enough to uncover lower slopes and that vegetation was reviving. The narrative states the inference directly: “so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth.” The dove had completed exactly the mission given in verse 8, and the wording of the result repeats the wording of the commission.

The olive tree held a special place in Israel’s life. Its oil lit the sanctuary lamp (Exodus 27:20), anointed priests and kings, and became an emblem of fruitfulness and blessing. The psalmist pictured the righteous as “a green olive tree in the house of God” (Psalm 52:8), and Zechariah saw two olive trees feeding the lampstand with oil by God’s Spirit (Zechariah 4:3, 6). The later image of a dove with an olive branch as a sign of peace grows from this verse, though the text itself presents the leaf as a sign of returning life on a judged earth.

That sign came from God, delivered by a small creature at the close of an ordinary day. Throughout his time in the ark Noah received no recorded word from heaven. He learned of the earth’s renewal through a bird and a leaf. God is not limited to speaking audibly; He can make His faithfulness known through the ordinary workings of the world He governs.

For the believer, the olive leaf has become a reminder that God’s judgments are never His last word for those He has sheltered. Life springs up on the other side. The same God who preserved a single tree beneath the flood will raise His people to life on a renewed earth.

wordNotes.term: עֲלֵה־זַיִת טָרָף (ʿaleh-zayit taraf) — an olive leaf pluckt off
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective taraf normally describes something torn, as prey is torn by a beast. Applied to a leaf, it means freshly plucked from a growing tree. The point is that the leaf was alive and green, proof that olive trees on lower ground were above water and putting out new growth.

wordNotes.term: לְעֵת עֶרֶב (leʿet ʿerev) — in the evening
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “at the time of evening,” the hour when birds return to roost. The phrase also marks the close of a day, the boundary that Genesis 1 uses to order time. The dove’s return at this hour fits a bird that had spent a full day outside.

verses.bibleText: And he stayed yet other seven days; and sent forth the dove; which returned not again unto him any more.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After another seven days Noah released the dove a third time, and she “returned not again unto him any more.” Her absence was the final report. She had found food and shelter in a world able to sustain life, and she stayed there.

The pattern of three releases, each separated by a week, moves from no rest, to a sign of life, to a new home. The dove’s silence spoke as clearly as the olive leaf. Noah now had good evidence that the earth was recovering. Yet the narrative will show in the next verses that evidence alone did not determine his next step. He waited for God.

The weekly rhythm of these flights is worth noticing again. Noah’s waiting was measured in sevens, the cycle God had marked at creation. Within the confinement of the ark, the family kept time by the week God had given, and the rhythm ended with the bird going out into a renewed creation. God’s order of time persisted through the judgment, ready for life to resume.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא־יָסְפָה שׁוּב־אֵלָיו עוֹד (welo-yasefah shuv-ʾelayw ʿod) — which returned not again unto him any more
wordNotes.explanation: The verb yasaf, “to add, do again,” with “return” and “any more,” stresses finality: the dove never came back. Its absence is the final piece of evidence that the earth had become habitable, the last report in the sequence of bird flights.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried up from off the earth: and Noah removed the covering of the ark, and looked, and, behold, the face of the ground was dry.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A new date heads the verse: “the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month.” Noah had entered the flood in his six hundredth year (7:6, 11). Now, on the first day of a new year, “the waters were dried up from off the earth.” The opening of a year was later the day Moses set up the tabernacle (Exodus 40:2, 17) and the day Hezekiah began cleansing the temple (2 Chronicles 29:17). It is a fitting moment for a fresh beginning on a cleansed earth.

Noah “removed the covering of the ark, and looked.” The covering was part of the roof, perhaps made of skins or similar material. The same Hebrew word names the outer covering of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:14) and the wrappings placed over the sanctuary furniture for travel (Numbers 4:10–12). The ark that carried God’s people safely through judgment shares a vocabulary with the sanctuary where God would later dwell among His people. Without pressing the link too hard, the echo invites readers to see both as structures of divine provision and protection.

What Noah saw confirmed what the dove had reported: “behold, the face of the ground was dry.” The “face of the ground” is the very surface from which God had said He would blot out every living thing (6:7; 7:4, 23). It now lies open again, scrubbed by judgment and ready to be lived on. The word “behold” lets the reader stand beside Noah and share his first broad look at the new world.

Yet the surface was only beginning to dry. The verb in this verse describes waters drained away, leaving ground that was no longer flooded but not yet firm. Noah could see the earth, but he still did not step out. The next verse explains why another eight weeks passed.

wordNotes.term: מִכְסֵה (mikseh) — covering
wordNotes.explanation: A covering or roof layer, from a verb meaning to cover. In the Pentateuch it names the outer covering of skins over the tabernacle and the protective wrappings for the sanctuary furnishings. Here Noah removes part of the ark’s roof covering to see the land below.

wordNotes.term: חָרְבוּ (charvu) — were dried up
wordNotes.explanation: The verb charav means to become dry or drained of water, as when the Red Sea and the Jordan became passable. It describes the disappearance of standing water from the surface, a step before the ground became fully firm in verse 14.

verses.bibleText: And in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, was the earth dried.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, was the earth dried.” A different verb is used here from the one in verse 13. There the waters had drained away from the surface; here the earth itself has become dry and firm. The word is related to “the dry land” that God called forth on the third day of creation (1:9–10). The land of Genesis 1, buried in the flood, now stands fully restored.

The date closes the flood’s calendar. Counting from the onset of the rain in Noah’s six hundredth year, month two, day seventeen (7:11), to this date in year six hundred and one, month two, day twenty-seven, the earth stood dry again. That span is a year and ten days, or roughly the length of a solar year if the months were lunar. Whatever calendar lies behind it, the family spent more than a full year inside the ark.

The eight weeks between verses 13 and 14 show Noah’s restraint. He could see dry ground, but God had shut the door (7:16), and Noah would not open it on his own authority.

wordNotes.term: יָבְשָׁה (yaveshah) — was dried
wordNotes.explanation: From yavesh, “to be dry,” the root behind yabbashah, “dry land,” in Genesis 1:9–10 and in the crossing of the Red Sea. Its use here signals that the land is not merely uncovered but solid again, restored to the condition God gave it at creation.

verses.bibleText: And God spake unto Noah, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God spake unto Noah, saying.” These few words break a long silence. The last recorded divine speech came before Noah entered the ark (7:1–4). Through the months of rain, drifting, grounding, and waiting, no word from God is reported. Noah gathered what he could from birds and his own eyes. Now God speaks again, and the timing belongs to Him.

The verse also explains Noah’s delay in verses 13–14. He had evidence enough that the ground was dry, but he waited for this. The man who built the ark because God told him to (6:22; 7:5) leaves it for the same reason. His whole story runs from one divine command to the next.

wordNotes.term: וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים (waydabber ʾelohim) — and God spake
wordNotes.explanation: The verb dibber, “to speak,” introduces formal divine address. Elsewhere in the flood story God “said” to Noah; this fuller verb marks the decisive word that ends the confinement. The same verb introduces the Ten Commandments, God’s speech that structures His people’s life.

verses.bibleText: Go forth of the ark, thou, and thy wife, and thy sons, and thy sons' wives with thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Go forth of the ark, thou, and thy wife, and thy sons, and thy sons’ wives with thee.” The command answers the earlier one: “Come thou and all thy house into the ark” (7:1). God called the family in, and God calls them out. The listing of the household mirrors 6:18 and 7:13 almost exactly, a quiet assurance that every person who entered left alive. Peter would later count them: “few, that is, eight souls were saved by water” (1 Peter 3:20).

The ark was a refuge, not a permanent dwelling. It served its purpose for a year, carrying God’s people across judgment from the old world to the new. Its door had been shut by the LORD Himself (7:16), and the family could not leave until He released them. The departure therefore rests on God’s authority as much as the entrance did.

Noah’s patience here deserves notice. He had spent decades building the ark and warning his generation (2 Peter 2:5), then more than a year inside it, through storm and stillness. He had seen the dove fly free and the ground dry under the open roof. Still he waited until the word came. That restraint is the obedience of faith Hebrews commends: Noah acted, and refrained from acting, according to what God had told him (Hebrews 11:7).

The scene also anticipates a greater going forth. Those preserved through the final judgment will step out onto a new earth at God’s word, when the One who shut the door of grace opens the door to the inheritance prepared for them (Revelation 21:1–5).

wordNotes.term: צֵא (tse) — go forth
wordNotes.explanation: The simple imperative of yatsa, “to go out,” the same word God used to call Abram from Haran and the verb that dominates Israel’s exodus from Egypt. Here it releases Noah from the ark into a new world. The verb recurs four times in verses 16–19, giving the passage its theme of exit.

verses.bibleText: Bring forth with thee every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth; that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Noah is to bring out “every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh,” and the categories follow the order of creation: fowl, cattle, and every creeping thing. The purpose is life: “that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth.” These are the words of the blessing God spoke over the creatures on the fifth day: “Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth” (1:22). The same commission is spoken again in a cleansed world.

The verb “breed abundantly” is the word used in Genesis 1 for the swarming of living creatures in the waters (1:20–21). It suggests teeming, prolific life. Later it describes Israel multiplying in Egypt in spite of Pharaoh’s oppression (Exodus 1:7). God’s will for His creation, even after judgment, is fullness of life.

This stands in sharp contrast with the outlook of the Mesopotamian flood traditions, where the gods afterward devised ways to limit human numbers and the hero looked out on a world turned to clay. Genesis presents a Creator who judged violence and corruption but never stopped desiring a living, fruitful earth.

The responsibility given to Noah is significant. He does not simply open the door and step aside; God tells him to “bring forth” the animals with him. As the first man was set over the creatures to care for them (1:26–28; 2:15, 19), so Noah, a second father of humanity, shepherds them out into their renewed habitats. The care he showed for the dove now extends to every species entrusted to him.

wordNotes.term: וְשָׁרְצוּ (wesharetsu) — that they may breed abundantly
wordNotes.explanation: The verb sharats means to swarm or teem, used in Genesis 1:20–21 for the abundance of creatures in the waters and in Exodus 1:7 for Israel’s rapid increase. It pictures life spreading in great numbers, the reversal of the death that swept the earth in the flood.

wordNotes.term: וּפָרוּ וְרָבוּ (uparu weravu) — and be fruitful, and multiply
wordNotes.explanation: The paired verbs of the creation blessing, spoken to creatures on the fifth day and to humanity on the sixth. Their repetition here and in 9:1 signals that God is renewing the original mandate of creation in the world after the flood.

verses.bibleText: And Noah went forth, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives with him:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Noah went forth, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons’ wives with him.” The fulfillment repeats the command almost word for word, the narrator’s regular way of showing Noah’s exact obedience (6:22; 7:5, 9, 16). Noah has still not spoken a recorded word in the entire flood narrative. His faith is seen in what he does.

The order shifts slightly from the command: the sons are named before the wife. Whatever the reason, the same eight people who went in come out. The God who shut them in had kept every one of them through the year.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּצֵא־נֹחַ (wayyetse-noach) — and Noah went forth
wordNotes.explanation: The narrative form of yatsa, “to go out,” directly answering the imperative “go forth” of verse 16. Hebrew narrative often shows obedience by echoing the command’s vocabulary, so the reader hears that Noah did exactly what God said.

verses.bibleText: Every beast, every creeping thing, and every fowl, and whatsoever creepeth upon the earth, after their kinds, went forth out of the ark.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The animals follow: “every beast, every creeping thing, and every fowl, and whatsoever creepeth upon the earth.” The comprehensive list confirms that the creatures who entered the ark all came out. None was lost. The narrator who counted the dead outside the ark (7:21–23) now counts the living who emerge.

They go out “after their kinds,” literally “by their families.” The word is the one used for clans and households of people. The animals leave the ark in orderly groups, each kind with its own, as they had been created “after their kind” (1:21, 24–25) and brought in the same way (7:14). The order God built into creation survived the flood and resumes on the renewed earth.

This detail also prepares for the next verse. Among these families of animals, some were clean and some unclean, a distinction Noah had observed when he took seven pairs of clean beasts into the ark (7:2). That distinction is about to govern his first act of worship.

wordNotes.term: לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתֵיהֶם (lemishpechotehem) — after their kinds (by their families)
wordNotes.explanation: Mishpachah normally means a clan or extended family, as in the families of the nations in Genesis 10 and the clans of Israel. Applied to animals, it presents them leaving the ark in family groups, each kind with its own, reflecting the ordered creation of Genesis 1.

verses.bibleText: And Noah builded an altar unto the LORD; and took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl, and offered burnt offerings on the altar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first thing Noah does on the renewed earth is worship. “Noah builded an altar unto the LORD.” Before he plants a field, builds a house, or explores the land, he sets up a place of sacrifice. This is the first altar named in Scripture, though not the first sacrifice; Abel had already brought the firstlings of his flock (4:4), and the skins with which God clothed Adam and Eve imply the death of animals at the very start of sin’s history (3:21). Noah carries forward that pattern of approaching God through offering, now on a world freshly delivered from judgment.

He “took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl.” This is why God had told him to bring seven pairs of clean animals but only one pair of the unclean (7:2–3). The extra clean animals made sacrifice possible without wiping out a species. The distinction between clean and unclean was therefore known and practiced long before Sinai. Leviticus 11 would later set it down in detail for Israel, but its roots reach back to God’s instruction to Noah, and it governed both what could be offered and, as 9:3 assumes, what humans would eat. The partitive wording, “of every clean beast,” indicates that Noah offered some from each clean kind, not every clean animal he had.

The offerings were “burnt offerings,” sacrifices wholly consumed on the altar. The Hebrew name pictures something going up, the smoke rising toward heaven. In Israel’s later worship the burnt offering was offered every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42) and was the basic act of approach to God. The worshiper laid a hand on the animal, which was accepted “to make atonement for him” (Leviticus 1:4). It expressed thanksgiving and full devotion, but it also confessed that sinners come to God only through a substitute that dies in their place. Noah had just seen what death outside God’s provision means. Now clean animals die on the altar, standing in for the family that grace had spared.

Each of those sacrifices pointed forward to Christ, “the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Noah’s worship rested on faith in God’s provision, the same faith that had moved him to build the ark (Hebrews 11:7). The altar on Ararat stands at the head of a line of altars raised by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (12:7–8; 26:25; 35:7), all of them looking toward the one offering that would fulfil them.

The priority Noah gave to worship is instructive. After a year of confinement, there were countless practical needs. He placed gratitude and consecration first, offering generously from animals that were scarce on an empty earth. Those who have been brought through God’s judgments are called to the same response: “present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God” (Romans 12:1).

wordNotes.term: מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach) — altar
wordNotes.explanation: The usual Hebrew word for an altar, formed from the verb for slaughtering a sacrifice, so it names the place where offerings were made. This is its first occurrence in Scripture. The patriarchs built simple altars of earth or uncut stone as places of worship and of calling on the LORD’s name.

wordNotes.term: עֹלֹת (ʿolot) — burnt offerings
wordNotes.explanation: Plural of ʿolah, from the verb ʿalah, “to go up,” describing the offering that went up wholly in smoke. It is the most frequent sacrifice in the Old Testament, offered in thanksgiving, dedication, and for atonement. Job offered such sacrifices for his children in case they had sinned.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD smelled a sweet savour.” The language is deliberately human. God does not breathe in smoke as a hungry deity would, and the contrast with the surrounding cultures is stark. In the Babylonian flood story the gods, starved during the deluge because no humans were left to feed them, crowded around the hero’s sacrifice like flies. Genesis has nothing of that. The phrase “sweet savour” became the standard term in Leviticus for an offering God accepts (Leviticus 1:9, 13, 17). It means that God received Noah’s worship with favor. Through Noah’s offering, the God whose heart had been grieved by human violence (6:6) is pleased.

The New Testament applies the same phrase to Christ: “Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour” (Ephesians 5:2). Noah’s animals could not themselves remove sin (Hebrews 10:4). What made them acceptable was the sacrifice they foreshadowed and the faith with which they were offered. God’s delight in the offering on Ararat points to His perfect delight in the self-giving of His Son.

“And the LORD said in his heart.” What follows is not yet spoken to Noah; it is God’s inner resolve, revealed to the reader. It answers the earlier passage where the LORD saw human wickedness and “it grieved him at his heart” (6:6). The resolve has two parts. “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake,” and “neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.” The curse of 3:17 is not withdrawn; thorns, toil, and death remain, as all human experience confirms. What God renounces is another universal destruction like the flood. Local disasters still occur, but the world as a whole will not again be swept away by water (9:11; Isaiah 54:9).

The reason given is startling: “for the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” In 6:5 the same diagnosis was the reason for judgment. Here it accompanies the promise of restraint. The KJV margin suggests “though,” and the clause may be read as a concession: even though human nature is corrupt, God will not respond again with total destruction. Read as a cause, it means that another flood would solve nothing, since judgment removed sinners without changing the heart. Only grace can carry the world forward.

The heart is bent toward evil “from his youth,” from the earliest stage of life (Psalm 51:5; Jeremiah 17:9). God’s answer is not to lower His standard but to provide a sacrifice and, in time, a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26). The promise of patience that began at Noah’s altar keeps the world alive so that the gospel may be preached and sinners may repent before the final judgment, which Scripture says will come by fire (2 Peter 3:7, 9).

wordNotes.term: רֵיחַ הַנִּיחֹחַ (reach hannichoach) — a sweet savour
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the aroma of soothing” or “restful aroma,” from nuach, “to rest,” echoing Noah’s name. The phrase recurs throughout Leviticus and Numbers for offerings God accepts. The Septuagint’s rendering, osmē euōdias, is the phrase Paul uses of Christ’s self-offering and of the believers’ gifts.

wordNotes.term: יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם (yetser lev haʾadam) — the imagination of man’s heart
wordNotes.explanation: Yetser comes from a verb meaning to form or shape, as a potter shapes clay. It denotes the inclination or shaping purpose of the mind. The same term appears in 6:5. Scripture uses it of the settled bent of thought and will, which only God can know and renew.

verses.bibleText: While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God’s inner resolve closes with a short poem: “While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.” Four pairs of opposites cover the whole cycle of the year and the day. Each pair names two extremes to embrace everything between them. The rhythms that the flood had interrupted for a year will continue without another universal break.

These rhythms go back to creation. On the fourth day God set lights in the sky “for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years” (1:14), and from the first day He separated light from darkness, evening from morning (1:4–5). The flood had seemed to undo that order, returning the earth to watery formlessness. God now pledges that it will stand. Jeremiah later used this very promise as the measure of God’s faithfulness: if anyone could break God’s covenant with the day and the night, then His covenant with David could be broken too (Jeremiah 33:20–21, 25–26). Every sunrise and every harvest is a quiet testimony that God keeps His word.

The promise also speaks to human labour. “Seedtime and harvest” recalls the toil laid on Adam when the ground was cursed (3:17–19). Work remains hard, but it will not be futile; the farmer may sow with confidence that the season for reaping will come. Paul preached this to pagans at Lystra, pointing to “rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons” as God’s witness to Himself (Acts 14:17), and Jesus spoke of the Father who sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

Yet the promise carries a limit: “while the earth remaineth,” literally “all the days of the earth.” It does not say that the present world will last forever. Scripture teaches that “the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment” (2 Peter 3:7). God’s patience in sustaining the seasons serves His purpose of salvation, “not willing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). At the close of this age Christ will return visibly in glory, and the world will be judged, not again by water but by fire, and then made new. In that renewed creation the rhythm of night and toil will give way to a new order where “there shall be no night there” (Revelation 22:5).

The verb “cease” is the same Hebrew word used when God ceased from His work on the seventh day (2:2–3). The God who rested at creation now guarantees that the order He established will not rest from its course until His purpose is complete. Genesis 8 ends, then, with a promise worth trusting: the God who remembered Noah sustains the world day by day, and He will finish what He began.

wordNotes.term: עֹד כָּל־יְמֵי הָאָרֶץ (ʿod kol-yeme haʾarets) — while the earth remaineth
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “yet all the days of the earth.” The phrase sets a boundary on the promise: it lasts for the duration of the present earth. Comparable expressions, “all the days of thy life,” mark a lifespan that will end. The promise guarantees stability for this age, not the endless continuation of the present order.

wordNotes.term: לֹא יִשְׁבֹּתוּ (lo yishbotu) — shall not cease
wordNotes.explanation: From shavat, “to stop, cease, rest,” the verb used in Genesis 2:2–3 when God “rested” on the seventh day and the root of the noun Sabbath. Here it is negated: the cycles of nature will not stop. The same God who ceased from creating promises that the order He made will not cease.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it mean for God to “remember” someone who has been shut in and waiting for months?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The God who judged the world remembers His people, renews His creation, and receives worship offered through sacrifice, binding Himself by grace to preserve the earth until His final purpose is complete.
discussionQuestions: How does the wind over the waters in 8:1 echo Genesis 1:2, and what does that suggest about God’s purpose after judgment?
Why did Noah wait for God’s command after he could already see the ground was dry?
What does the distinction between clean and unclean animals in 8:20 show about God’s instruction before Sinai?
How can the same evil human heart be a reason for judgment in 6:5 and the occasion for restraint in 8:21?
How does the promise of 8:22 shape the way we view the seasons and the future of the earth?
commonMisunderstandings: God’s remembering Noah does not mean He had forgotten him; it means God acted on His covenant commitment.
The promise not to curse the ground again does not cancel the curse of Genesis 3:17; it rules out another universal destruction by water.
The pledge that the seasons will continue “while the earth remaineth” is not a promise that this present world will last forever unchanged.
The pleasing aroma does not picture God needing food or being manipulated; it expresses His acceptance of sacrifice offered in faith.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God as the main actor: He remembers, sends the wind, seals the waters, speaks the command, and accepts the offering. Noah’s patience and worship matter because they answer what God has done.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Wait for the Lord’s word as Noah did, and let your first response to every deliverance be worship that rests on the one Sacrifice God has fully accepted.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God remembers those sheltered in His provision, accepts the sacrifice that points to Christ, and preserves the world by grace until the day of final judgment and renewal.
flow: The flood showed that God takes sin seriously and that judgment is real.
God remembered Noah and brought him safely through, because He had provided the ark and made a covenant.
Noah’s first act was worship through a substitute sacrifice that God accepted.
God’s patience in sustaining the seasons gives every person time to repent.
The same God who ended the flood will end this age at Christ’s appearing; refuge is found in Him now.
simpleIllustrations: A rescuer who says “I remember you” is not recalling a name; he is coming back for the person he promised to save.
Every harvest is a reminder written into the calendar that God is still keeping a promise made to Noah.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you come into God’s provided refuge in Christ while He still holds back the final judgment in patience?
cautions: Do not turn every detail of the raven and dove into allegory; let the text’s own emphasis on patience and evidence lead.
Do not use the promise of 8:22 to deny that the world will meet a final judgment by fire.
Do not imply that Noah’s sacrifice earned God’s favor apart from grace.

reflectionQuestions: When have I felt shut in and forgotten, and how does “God remembered Noah” speak to that season?
Am I willing to wait for God’s direction even when the ground already looks dry to me?
What would it look like for worship to be my first act after God brings me through a trial?
How does the regular return of seedtime and harvest remind me of God’s patience toward me?
Where am I relying on my own improvement instead of on the sacrifice God has accepted?
